list.listitem: Consider osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) in the young to middle-aged patient with acute knee or ankle trauma that is not improving as expected or in the patient with repetitive overuse injury and chronic, nonspecific joint complaints. C
Obtain plain radiographs on all patients suspected of having OCD; consider MRI when plain films are non-diagnostic or for staging. C
Conservative management should be the first line treatment for any young patient who has a stable lesion and open physis. C
Non-operative treatment is rarely attempted in adults or adolescents with a closed physis due to a propensity to progress to unstable lesions and early operative referral is generally indicated. C

The overall prognosis for young patients with OCD, regardless of treatment method, is favorable while prognosis for patients treated surgically is improved by early operative treatment and the use of advanced surgical techniques. C

background.definition: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) is an acquired, potentially reversible idiopathic lesion of subchondral bone resulting in delamination and sequestration with or without articular cartilage involvement and instability.

list.listitem: Annual incidence of OCD in the general population is estimated to be 15 to 30 cases per 100,000 perons.
Males affected at a ratio of 5:3 over females although the incidence in females is thought to be rising due to increased sports participation at younger ages.

The overall age and sex adjusted incidence of OCD of the knee is 6 per 100,000 persons in Olmsted County, Minnesota, USA. The incidence was 8.8 per 100,000 in males and 3.3 per 100,000 in females. Incidence peaked at 11 to 15 year of age.
Most common cause of a loose body in the joint space in adolescent patients.
Felt to be multifactorial yet etiology remains unclear.
Theories exist including the following causes: traumatic, ischemic, hereditary, and idiopathic.
A commonly suggested etiology is repetitive microtrauma comprised of shear and compressive forces as seen in athletic persons.
OCD lesions may be caused by acute trauma; common associations include ACL tears or ankle inversion injuries.
Childhood obesity is associated with an increased risk of OCD of the elbow and ankle (OR 3.0) and extreme obesity with OCD of the knee (OR 1.8).
Based upon repetitive trauma model, recurrent micro-injury results in a stress reaction leading to stress fracture in the underlying subchondral bone.
Softening of the articular cartilage can occur which contributes to the damage to subchondral bone.
Repetitive loading persists and exceeds the ability of the underlying bone to heal, leading to necrosis and fragment dissection, separation, and nonunion.
May also be an acute injury following a specific trauma (for example, OCD lesions have been reported in up to 80% of anterior cruciate ligament ruptures).

Consider OCD in the young to middle-age patient with acute knee or ankle trauma that is not improving as expected or in the patient with repetitive overuse of the knee, ankle, or elbow with chronic, nonspecific joint complaints. C
Plain radiographs should be obtained on all patients suspected of having OCD and MRI may be considered when plain films are non-diagnostic or for staging. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Children aged 4-8 years, involves entire ossific nucleus of capitellum, self-limiting
Active patients or degenerative changes in adults, associated with swelling, stiffness, and pain when knee is rotated
Associated with running and jumping exercises, pain around patella worsened with walking up and down stairs, squatting, or prolonged sitting
Teen and young adult patients; anterior knee pain with associated clicking, popping, edema, or instability of patello-femoral joint
Typically overweight adolescent patients; associated with pain in groin, hip, and sometimes knee; patient may walk with a limp or with affected leg turned outward
Pediatric patients; decreased blood supply to hip joint associated with pain and stiffness in hip, knee, or groin, and worse with activity, improves with rest

list.listitem: Nonspecific and poorly localized pain in the affected joint is the most common presenting symptom. OCD is rarely seen before age 10 years or after age 50 years; most commonly diagnosed between ages 12 and 20 years.
The knee is involved in 75% of cases followed by the ankle and elbow, less commonly affected are the patella, femoral head, scapular glenoid, and tibial plateau. Up to 25% of cases are bilateral.

Common complaints include joint swelling, stiffness, and pain that are exacerbated by exercise. The clinical exam is moderately sensitive and very specific for making the diagnosis (LR+ 39, LR− 0.23).Mechanical symptoms such as locking or catching may indicate unstable or loose fragments.

Examination of the knee may be nonspecific; findings may include an effusion, decreased range of motion, antalgic gait, and a positive Wilson's sign (the knee is flexed to 90 degrees, the tibia internally rotated, and then slowly extended - increased pain at approximately 30 degrees of flexion is considered positive).

OCD lesions of the ankle often present with an antalgic gait and joint swelling; pain may be elicited with ankle inversion or tibial talar compression and tenderness to palpation may be found posterior to the medial malleolus with the ankle in dorsiflexion or anterior to the lateral malleolus with the ankle in plantarflexion.

The elbow affected by OCD may demonstrate an effusion with tenderness to palpation over the capitellum and lateral elbow; a restricted range of motion may be present with a lack of terminal extension the most frequent finding.
Arthroscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis, however radiographic studies are usually employed first to allow for non-invasive evaluation.
Plain radiographs are the initial study of choice for evaluating suspected OCD lesions of any joint.

Routine views of the joint should be obtained; sensitivity and specificity of plain films varies, up to 70% of acute talar OCD lesions can be identified with plain radiographs; elbow films demonstrate only partial involvement of the capitellum.

When plain films are non-diagnostic and for further non-invasive evaluation of OCD, MRI may be used for identification and staging to enable treatment strategies and prognosis (see ); for children and adolescents, MRI is 91% sensitive and 98% specific for diagnosis of OCD.

Other less commonly used radiographic modalities include bone scan (very sensitive early in the course following an injury), CT (useful for identifying loose bodies), and MRI arthrography (may allow for more accurate determination of the status of the overlying cartilage).

Suspect OCD in patients with acute trauma whose symptoms are not improving as expected (patellar dislocation or anterior cruciate ligament tear of the knee or sprain or fracture of the ankle) and in patients with a long history of overuse who have chronic, nonspecific joint complaints and intermittent swelling of the knee, ankle, and elbow.

Plain radiographs should be obtained on all patients suspected of having OCD and MRI may be considered when plain radiographs are non-diagnostic or for staging. In one study, MR imaging criteria for OCD instability had higher specificity in adults than for children and adolescents.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Treatment decisions are based on clinical findings and symptoms, skeletal age and maturity, and lesion characteristics including size, location, and stability. C

Conservative (non-operative) management should be the first line treatment for any young patient who has a stable lesion and open physis and may consist of limited weight bearing, immobilization, restriction from the offending activity, and physical therapy. C
Non-operative management is rarely attempted in adults or adolescents with a closed physis due to the propensity to progress to unstable lesions and early operative referral is generally indicated. C

Surgical intervention is used in patients who have failed conservative management or patients with an unstable lesion and/or a closed physis to maintain joint congruity, fixation of unstable or loose fragments, and repair osteochondral defects. C

Surgical treatment may involve arthroscopy to perform lavage, debridement, fixation, and marrow stimulation or open arthrotomy for advanced surgical techniques such as osteochondral autograft transplantation (OATS) fixation, microfracture, and autologous chondroycte implantation (ACI). B
Intraarticular steroid injections have not been shown to have a beneficial effect on healing of lesions of the talus.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) may be used to achieve symptom relief but the benefit must be weighed against the theoretical risk of the negative effect of NSAIDS on bone healing and interfering with monitoring of disease progression; acetaminophen may be used for symptom relief without the NSAID-associated risk.
In patients who use pain medication for symptomatic treatment, it is advised to record days with swelling and days without and compare to daily activity to assess compliance to treatment plans.
In addition to pain medication, activity modification and weight control remain the mainstay treatment.
If pain is persistent despite adherence to activity modifications and acetaminophen, more aggressive intervention may be warranted.

Surgical management should be considered in all patients who have failed conservative management including stable (immobile) lesions. Early operative treatment is generally indicated for all patients with an unstable (immobile) lesion and/or a closed physis.
This was confirmed by a systematic review that found non-operative management to be similar to surgical for low-grade lesions, but that surgery was superior for high grade or unstable lesions.
Given the loss of vascular supply and fibrous tissue in subchondral bone in skeletally mature patients, lesions in this population will most often require surgical treatment.
Goals of surgical management are to maintain joint congruity, fixation of unstable or loose fragments, and repair of osteochondral defects. Long term goals include prevention of early arthritis.
Surgical treatment is usually through arthroscopy to identify lesion stability and may include drilling and internal fixation.

The knee is the most common site to require surgical intervention, with roughly 58% of all OCD procedures being performed on the knee. The standard surgical treatment of the knee with intact cartilage that has failed conservative management is drilling.

If there is concern about stability, internal fixation is necessary with drilling. This is typically accomplished with cannulated screws, Herbert screws, bone pegs, metal staples, or other bio-absorbable implants. A review of 24 patients with unstable OCD that were treated with bioabsorable devices illustrated 22 of 24 patients with good-to-excellent outcomes. A review of 13 small studies showed no significant differences in outcome between fixation type.

A systematic review of 24 studies of surgical procedures for unstable OCD of the knee concluded that internal fixation was preferred for skeletally immature patients, while in skeletally mature patients autologous chondrocyte implantation and osteochondral allograft transplantation provided the best outcomes.

A sytematic review of case series identified 35 reports of arthroscopic debridement with fragment fixation in OCD of the humeral capitellum and 107 reports of open procedures, with generally similar outcomes.

A systematic review of femoral trochlear OCD found a total of 105 patients in case series and reports. A total of 75% received operative management, with 82% where the open procedure was known having open reduction internal fixation, and 31% receiving arthroscopic procedures having arthroscopic reduction internal fixation or drilling. Fully 93% reported return to sports.
A review of case series of 136 young athletes undergoing arthroscopic microfracture for OCD of the capitellum (elbow) found return to sports in 60% to 100% at the previous level of competition.

Advanced surgical techniques that may require open arthrotomy include salvage procedures such as autogenous osteochondral plugs, hybrid fixation with osteochondral autograft transplantation (OATS) fixation, microfracture, and autologous chondroycte implantation (ACI). This is typically reserved for patients who fail to heal, have multiple small fragments, with excessively deteriorated cartilage, or an incongruous fragment with the donor site.
Autogenous osteochondral plugs are considered an alternative to implantable screws. The plugs allow for bone grafting in addition to lesion fixation.

Microfracture is a marrow stimulation technique that allows pluripotent stem cells from the preserved subchondral bone into the marrow of the osteochondral defect and results in formation of fibrocartilage. This is typically reserved for patients with a localized, small cartilage defect.

OATS fixation is indicated for younger patients where the defect is larger (typically 1-4 cm2) and subchondral bone is not present, requiring replacement with normal hyaline cartilage. It allows osteochondral fragment preservation in patients with unstable femoral condylar OCD lesions. This technique is thought to be a hybrid fixation that includes screws and osteochondral autograft transplant; typically both articular cartilage and subchondral bone from a non-weight bearing area of the knee are relocated to the site defect.

In a randomized trial of 50 participants, median age of 14.3 years, when comparing microfracture versus OATS outcomes, both groups had good-to-excellent results at the 1 year mark. At more than 4 years, OATS patients maintained 83% good-to-excellent results where microfracture was 63%. Failure rates were 0% in OATS group and 41% in the microfracture group.

ACI is a more invasive appropach typically used in contained (up to 10 cm2), irreparable lesions. It requires two separate procedures, the first is harvesting a cartilage biopsy and allowing ex vivo expansion and the second is implantation.

Osteochondral allograft transplantation is reserved for large lesions (>3 cm2) and avoids donor site morbidity. In a study of 135 patients aged 12 to 55 years of age, 5 year survivorship was 95% and 10 year survivorship was 93%.
A systematic review identified 7 case series of ACI in athletes and found 94% returning to competitive sports in a mean time for unrestricted activity of 5.6 months (range 3 to 14 months).

A case series reported 27 patients undergoing cell-free osteochondral scaffold implantation for knee OCD. At 2 years, a knee-specific symptom score improved from a mean of 48 to 82 points, and then remained stable for up to 5 years.

Orally administered glucosamine has been shown to potentially have some benefit for knee joint pain relief when taken for twelve weeks at a dose of 2000 mg per day; the improvement in symptoms is generally seen by the eighth week of therapy.

Glycosaminoglycans given orally in combination with free radical scavengers (vitamin E and selenium) have been demonstrated in an animal model to improve healing of osteochondritis dissecans lesions treated non-surgically.
Nonsurgical management should be the first line treatment for any young patient who has a stable lesion and open physes.

Conservative management may consist of protected weight bearing with crutches, immobilization (casting, bracing, splinting, unloader brace), temporarily restricting the sporting or other event causing the repetitive microtrauma, and physical therapy for the restoration and maintenance of range of motion.

In a retrospective study of 298 skeletally immature patients, unloader bracing was used in 56% of patients for a minimum of 3 months compared to a group of 44% treated with other non-invasive, non-unloader treatment modalities. The unloader bracing group more often required surgical intervention when compared to the non-unloader group (50% vs 35% respectively), illustrating that unloader bracing is not associated with significantly improved outcomes compared to other non-operative management.
An estimated 50% to 67% of juvenile OCD lesions will heal in 6-12 months with non-operative managment.
An MRI may be repeated after 3 to 4 months to assess healing.
Non-operative management is rarely attempted in adults and adolescents with closed physes due to a decrease in healing ability.

Orthopedic referral should be considered in any young patient with an unstable lesion or who has failed non-surgical treatment and all adults, given the propensity for adult OCD lesions to be unstable and fail conservative management.

The overall prognosis for young patients with OCD is favorable, whether treated conservatively or eventually referred for operative management. The rate of return to sport for children and adolescents was 97.6% in a systematic review.C
Early idenitifcation and treatment is crucial; if left untreated there is an increased risk of osteoarthritis. Additional complications include chronic pain and non-union. B
Prognosis for successful non-operative treatment of juvenile OCD was better among those with smaller cyst-like lesions. B

Prognosis for patients treated surgically is improved by young age, open physis, earlier operative treatment when indicated, and the use of advanced surgical techniques. General consensus remains that stable lesion outcomes are more favorable than unstable lesions. B

In a case series of 175 patients with osteochondrosis of the humeral capitellum, 101 followed a conservative approach of avoidance of heavy elbow use for 6 months. Outcomes were good with healing in 90.5% of patients with stage I lesions (mean age 11.5 years) and in 52.9% of patients with stage II lesions (mean age 13.9 years). The mean period required for healing was 14.9 months in stage I and 12.3 months in stage II and most returned to competitive-level baseball (78.6% of stage I patients and 52.9% of stage II patients).
Return to sports participation depends on recovery time, and activity restriction is based on the treatment modailty utilized with an average estimated time of 3-6 months.

A review study was conducted on 258 patients who underwent surgical treatment for their OCD lesion. All were active athletes prior to their treatment. The analysis illustrated longer symptom duration correlated with more severe OCD lesions. Lesion severity was also found to correlate with time to return to sports participation, however did not corelate with overall ability to return to baseline activity. The mean patient age was 14 and mean symptom duration was 20.9 months.
A systematic review found mostly case series and no clear evidence that one surgical technique was superior to any other.
A systematic review found that there was a trend toward improved outcomes with more aggressive treatment of lateral lesions, which had a higher failure rate.

algorithm.title: Evaluation and Management of Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Knee.

cell.label: Suspected OCD of knee. Obtain posteroanterior, lateral, and tunnel-view radiographs.
Obtain radiographs of contralateral knee and MRI to determine stage of lesion.
Conservative measures: Stop competitive sports for 6 to 8 weeks. Low-intensity physical rehabilitation Goal: symptom-free activities of daily living.
Discharge patient to self-monitoring of symptoms.
Failure to improve, symptoms worsen or crepitus develops.
Orthopedic referral for arthroscopy to evaluate overlying cartilage.
Orthopedic referral for arthroscopy or open removal.
Search for other cause of knee pain.

feature.caption: MRI Staging of Joints with Osteochondritis Dissecans.
feature.feature_body:
Stage 0 − normal
Stage 1 − signal changes consistent with articular cartilage injury, without disruption, and normal subchondral bone (stable)
Stage 2 − high signal intensity breach of articular cartilage but stable subchondral bone fragment (stable)
Stage 3 − partial chondral attachment with high signal rim behind osteochondral fragment (unstable)
Stage 4 − loose body in the center of the osteochondral bed or free in the joint space (unstable)
MRI, magnetic resonance imaging.
Data from Loredo R, Sanders TG. Imaging of osteochondral injuries. Clin Sports Med 2001;20(2):249–278.
